title: Press freedom and photojournalism
subtitle: 20th century
subject: art
description: From Cartier-Bresson to Nick Ut, news photography pins history down in a single image. Freedom, ethics, and media power in the same viewfinder.

hero.hook: A photograph can help stop a war, or it can lie. First someone has to be free to publish it.

blocks.text: Photojournalism was born when a picture could hold the news as firmly as an article. One frame can sum up a war, a famine, a victory.
But without press freedom, those images stay in a drawer.

[[Henri Cartier-Bresson]] worked out the idea of the “decisive moment”: the right place, the right instant, the right frame. [[Gerda Taro]], working alongside Capa, died covering the Spanish Civil War. Photojournalism has its martyrs.
Illustrated magazines and photo agencies turned the job into a profession. A reporter set out with a camera the way others set out with a notebook. The risk was physical.

blocks.caption: A Leica over the shoulder, the street as the assignment

blocks.text: In Vietnam, the photograph by [[Nick Ut]] of a girl burned by napalm shook public opinion. One image did not “end” the war on its own, but it made the human cost impossible to deny.
The big democracies protect the press, at least on paper. Dictatorships control the viewfinder instead. The freedom to publish an image became a political barometer.
Many famous shots were censored or fought over first, long before they turned into historical common sense.

[[The ethics of photojournalism]] raises hard questions. Can you frame someone's suffering? Can you retouch it? [[Media concentration and editorial independence]] also puts an independent eye at risk.
In the digital age, verification is not optional: metadata, reverse image search, context. A photo is still powerful, but it can be manipulated faster than ever.

blocks.caption: The reporter, a witness armed with a lens

blocks.text: In the age of social networks, everyone takes pictures. The need for images that are reliable, placed in context, and protected by the right to inform has never been greater.
To really grasp press freedom and photojournalism, keep one thing in mind: every technical choice serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never merely decorative.
Context counts as much as style. Dates, places, patrons, audiences: all of it explains why a form appears at one precise moment and not before.
Finally, a legacy is measured over the long run. What we see today in museums, films, and popular music still carries the mark of these inventions.
Training the eye, defending whistleblowers, paying for reporting on the ground: without that, only the feed is left. The legacy of the 20th century is a demand, not nostalgia.
From Cartier-Bresson's Leica to the great war photographs, photojournalism proved that a free image can weigh as much as an editorial.
